origins.name: Obtained from the Town by records request

theirs.title: Published by the town, the district and the state
theirs.blurb: Primary documents. We did not write any of these and we did not commission them. 15 came from the Town by records request and say so on their row; the rest were already public. Where a document is unreadable or says something inconvenient, it is here anyway.

reference.title: Everything else the district and the town publish
reference.blurb: Mirrored here so it is available and so no figure has to be looked up over the network. 155 of these 170 feed no number on this site. The other 15 are byte-identical copies of primary sources listed above — kept, and marked as such on their row, because a mirror with the load-bearing documents quietly removed is no longer a copy of the publisher’s page. It is all here because a document nobody kept is a document nobody can check, and because we would rather hold what we did not use than be asked why we did not look.

ours.title: Written by this project, not by the town
ours.blurb: Everything below this line is ours. It is not town information, it carries no official standing, and nobody at the district or the Town has reviewed or approved it. It is one resident’s reading of the documents above, published so it can be argued with — which means checked against those documents, and disagreed with where the reading is wrong.

groups.title: The district budget, line by line
groups.blurb: The FY27 budget in every published version. Nearly every figure in this analysis traces to one of these five documents.

items.title: FY27 line-item projections, 23 March 2026
items.what: The version that carries the Level Service column, so all five scenarios sit side by side. This is the document that settles what "level service" cost.

items.title: FY27 proposed budget document, 25 March 2026
items.what: The printed line-item budget: FY26 final against the Restoration, Core and Balanced scenarios. 351 line items.

items.title: Multi-Scenario Financial Analysis
items.what: The narrative behind the four scenarios: what each one is, the cut and restoration lists, headcounts, impact statements, and the comparative summary. The source of every FTE count quoted here.

items.title: Additional Town Revenue Spending Plan
items.what: The $453,722 of positions added back at the September 2026 Special Town Meeting, with the district’s reasoning for each.

items.title: FY27 budget workbook, 25 March 2026
items.what: The richest single document here. 1,197 rows: FY23–FY25 actuals, FY26 final budget plus actuals-to-date and encumbrances, and all four FY27 scenarios. Every budget-line figure on this site comes from this workbook.

items.title: The same workbook, as circulated to the Finance Committee
items.what: Data-identical to the file above across every budget column; the differences are an unused scratch column and one ratio row. Kept so anyone working from the Finance Committee copy can confirm they match.

items.title: School Committee deck, 23 March 2026
items.what: Also image-only, and also unreadable without optical character recognition.

items.title: Balanced budget slide deck, 23 March 2026
items.what: Presented to the School Committee. Image-only — no text layer, so nothing in it could be quoted or checked.

items.title: FY27 line-item projections, 16 March 2026
items.what: An earlier draft with the restoration figures still in.

items.title: Earlier budget workbook, 24 February 2026
items.what: The 24 February version, before the restoration list was revised. Useful only for tracking what changed between drafts.

groups.title: Town budget, revenue and the override
groups.blurb: How much money the town has, where the Proposition 2½ formula puts the ceiling, and what happened at the ballot in May 2026.

items.title: Operating budgets: Balanced, Tier 1, Tier 2
items.what: The omnibus by department under all three funding scenarios — what each override tier would have bought, department by department.

items.title: Town Manager’s FY27 budget release, 17 April 2026
items.what: The revenue formula in full — levy limit, new growth, excluded debt, state aid, local receipts — plus all three budget scenarios by category, the cut lists and the tax impact per household. The backbone of the revenue model.

items.title: Election results, 16 May 2026
items.what: Both override questions defeated roughly two to one, in every precinct. Precinct-by-precinct tallies.

items.title: Annual Town Meeting booklet and warrant, 2026
items.what: The full 52-page warrant, including the revolving fund authorisations under Article 6.

items.title: Detailed town budget by line
items.what: Line-item town budget by organization and object code, including the Monty Tech assessment.

items.title: FY27 capital plan, Article 13
items.what: Capital requests, separate from the operating budget.

items.title: Ballot question language
items.what: The exact wording voters saw for both override questions.

groups.title: Quarterly financial reports, FY26 Q3
groups.blurb: The town’s financial position as of 31 March 2026, reported in August 2026 — the first quarterly report after a near-complete turnover of the finance office. This is where the funds held outside the operating budget appear.

items.title: Special revenue funds, 31 March 2026
items.what: Every special revenue and revolving fund the town holds, with opening balance, receipts, spending and closing balance. Includes the special education circuit breaker account, which appears in no budget document.

items.title: Trust, agency and stabilization funds, 31 March 2026
items.what: All stabilization and trust fund balances — general stabilization, OPEB, vehicle and equipment, conservation, and the rest.

items.title: Finance Director’s memo to the Finance Committee
items.what: The covering memo, dated 11 August 2026. Reports revenue and expenditure against budget, and gives the finance department’s own account of why quarterly reporting had lapsed.

items.title: General fund revenue, 31 March 2026
items.what: Revenue collected against budget by account. Local receipts came in at 116% of budget.

items.title: General fund expenditures, 31 March 2026
items.what: Spending against budget by department, including the school department line.

items.what: Self-supporting; does not bear on the school budget.

items.what: Self-supporting; does not bear on the school budget.

groups.title: School funds held outside the budget
groups.blurb: Revolving and gift accounts that belong to the schools but never appear in the operating appropriation. Obtained by records request, and a record of money actually received and spent rather than budgeted.

items.title: School gift, athletics and choice funds, FY26 year-end
items.what: Full-year reconciliation of three funds: opening balance, revenue by source, spending by category, closing balance. The only place actual athletics fee collections appear — $188,944 in FY26.

groups.title: Tax base, Chapter 70 and peers
groups.blurb: Where the town’s money comes from, what the state contributes, and how Lunenburg’s spending compares to its neighbors.

items.title: Tax Classification Hearing, FY2023
items.what: The single most valuable town document found. Carries year-by-year new growth FY18–FY23, assessed value by class, average single-family bills back to FY19, and excess levy capacity — series that appear nowhere else.

items.title: DESE per-pupil expenditures, FY2018–FY2024
items.what: Spending by category and per pupil, Lunenburg against eleven peer districts, with enrollment. Note: this is in-district expenditure, which by DESE’s definition excludes out-of-district tuition.

items.title: DESE Chapter 70 summary, FY27
items.what: Foundation enrollment, foundation budget, required local contribution, Chapter 70 aid and required net school spending, for every district in the state.

items.title: Finance Committee deck on Proposition 2½
items.what: Levy ceiling against levy limit against actual levy, and the state analysis showing assessed value outpacing the levy since 2017.

items.title: Board of Assessors agenda, 19 November 2025
items.what: Context on the classification process.

groups.title: Union contracts and salary schedules
groups.blurb: Where the 4% salary growth assumption comes from. Most are page scans, read with optical character recognition.

items.title: Lunenburg Education Association agreement
items.what: Runs 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2027. Raises of 2.5%, 4.0% and 3.5%, plus step increases worth about 3.32% a year. Expires at the end of FY27, so FY28 is the first year of an agreement nobody has negotiated.

items.title: Health insurance rates, 2025
items.what: Plan-by-plan premiums and the town’s 75/25 contribution split — the basis for every health insurance figure here.

items.title: Teacher salary schedule, FY25–FY27
items.what: Thirteen steps by ten lanes by three years, rebuilt from the printed FY25 grid and the contract’s own multipliers.

items.title: Custodial agreement, 2023–2026
items.what: The expiring custodial contract.

items.title: Paraprofessional agreement, FY26–FY28
items.what: Raises of 3.0%, 2.0% and 2.0%. Runs to 30 June 2028.

items.title: Custodial memorandum of agreement, 2026
items.what: Successor terms: 3.5%, 2.5%, 2.5% through FY29.

items.title: Paraprofessional salary schedule
items.what: The rate grid behind the agreement.

items.title: Administrator contract template
items.what: Also an expired DESE template, 2019–22.

items.title: Superintendent contract template
items.what: A DESE template from 2018–21, not a current Lunenburg agreement. No current administrator contract is public — a real gap.

items.what: Benefit terms for the same group.

items.what: Staff outside any bargaining unit.

groups.title: What neighboring districts did
groups.blurb: Primary FY27 budget documents from comparable districts. The comparison is only fair if it comes from their own books rather than from reporting.

items.title: Groton-Dunstable FY27 budget book
items.what: 132 pages. Three consecutive years of cuts, a budget below level service, and an override the district says is needed "now and in the foreseeable future". Also states plainly that it plans to offset $2M of costs with circuit breaker funding.

items.title: Ashburnham-Westminster FY27 budget
items.what: The district that made the opposite choice — explicitly preserved athletics, arts and music, and cut two elementary teaching positions instead.

items.title: North Middlesex budget summit notes
items.what: A $64,000 deficit at 3% growth against $1.5M at 5%. Roughly 30% of students receive special education, far above the state average.

items.title: Ashburnham-Westminster line detail
items.what: The line-item version of the same budget.

items.title: Ayer-Shirley FY27 expenses
items.what: Level-service budget by function. Health insurance up 14.4% — the steepest in the group.

items.title: Wachusett FY27 budget presentation
items.what: Member-town assessments, enrollment by town, and a discretionary contribution up 9.21%.

groups.title: Fees and program costs
groups.blurb: What families pay, and what the programs cost to run.

items.title: Athletic program costs by sport
items.what: Cost and participation for all 25 sports. The basis for every fee calculation on this site.

items.title: High school athletics fee schedule
items.what: The superseded schedule — $250, $140 and $85 with a $475 family cap. Still the only fee table published anywhere, though the fee rose to $400 for 2026-27. A family checking the website today gets the wrong number.

groups.title: Business registrations
groups.blurb: Town Clerk business certificate records, cleaned and categorised, behind the commercial growth argument.

items.title: Business certificate records
items.what: 711 records — certificate number, dates, name, owner, address, status and renewal chain. Note these are sole proprietor and partnership filings only; corporations register with the state and are not here.

items.title: Business records by industry
items.what: 554 records tagged by industry category, which is what shows that most new registrations are at residential addresses.

groups.title: Our analyses
groups.blurb: What we concluded, written up so it can be argued with. These are the only documents here we wrote — everything else in this archive was published by somebody else. Where one of them turned out to be wrong, the correction is in the document rather than quietly removed.

items.title: Special education and the curve
items.what: The FY27 level-service budget rises 3.98%. Strip out one line — out-of-district tuition, budgeted down 46% — and it rises 6.23%. What that one-off is doing to the rate, and what it risks for FY28. Budget columns only; no actual spending is used anywhere in it.

items.title: The FY27 budget and the override
items.what: Where things stand: the adopted budget, the four scenarios, what the balanced budget cut, the override result, the town’s revenue mechanics, and the first-cut FY28 arithmetic. The foundation the rest of this rests on.

items.title: Two right numbers: reconciling the FY27 cut
items.what: The FY27 budget was cut by $1,174,933 and by $761,000, and both are correct. A line-by-line bridge between them, and the three places the district’s own documents disagree with each other. Includes a correction to an earlier version of this analysis.

items.title: Special education and the funds outside the budget
items.what: Special education as a cost driver, out-of-district tuition, the circuit breaker account, and the school and town money held outside the operating appropriation. Carries a correction notice at the top — two growth figures in it were derived on a basis we no longer stand behind.

items.title: Budget versus actual
items.what: Did what the town budgeted match what it spent? Written for two readers — plain terms and the evidence, side by side. Deliberately separate from the app’s projection, and it says why. Unfinished: it names what it cannot see without the town’s accounting records.

items.title: What other districts did
items.what: The comparison across neighboring districts, and the order in which things actually get cut when an override fails.

groups.title: Built by this project
groups.blurb: Machine-readable extracts. Derived from the documents above and rebuildable from them.

items.title: Budget lines, tidy CSV
items.what: 356 rows extracted from the district workbook — section, function group, line item, and one column per fiscal year and scenario. Line sums tie to the printed totals within about $2 for FY25–FY27. Rebuild with scripts/extract_lps_budget.py.

items.title: Special education paraprofessionals, ten budgets
items.what: What the district budgeted for special education aides, FY18 to FY27, by school, read out of its own budget documents in the mirror above. Budget columns only, one budget stage held constant. The line grew 12.8% a year with an R-squared of 0.89 while the contract governing these staff gives 2.0% — which is the evidence the in-district escalator rests on. Rebuild with scripts/extract_budget_history.py.

items.title: Special education teachers, eight budgets
items.what: What the district budgeted for special education teachers, FY20 to FY27, by school. Grew 2.67% a year against a 3.5% agreement — below contract, which means fewer of them each year. The largest component of the in-district escalator, and the last one to stop being taken from a contract. Rebuild with scripts/extract_budget_history.py.

items.title: Out-of-district tuition, eleven budgets
items.what: What the district budgeted for out-of-district special education tuition, FY17 to FY27, read out of its own budget documents in the mirror above. Budget columns only, and one budget stage held constant throughout — a fiscal year has several budget figures for this line at different stages and they are far apart, so a series that took whichever number each document led with would be a walk across stages rather than a trend. Three of its years reproduce the FY27 workbook exactly. Rebuild with scripts/extract_tuition_history.py.

corpus.note: Every agenda and set of minutes the town publishes, across all boards. The scanned originals are not committed to the repository — they run to about 400MB and are re-fetchable — but the extracted text of all of them is, and that is what the analysis actually reads.

note: Every document this analysis is built on. Nothing here is private or paid for. 15 came from the Town by records request and are marked; the rest were published by the district, the town, the state or a neighboring district, and can be found again at the links above. Where a document was unreadable, or says something inconvenient, it is listed anyway.
